speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At this stage, the appellant need only set out the points of appeal briefly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Notice of Appeal is in a prescribed form which is contained in the Tribunal Rules, which only requires the appellant to state the grounds of his appeal in brief.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is only when the appellant files his Petition of Appeal, 21 days after serving the Notice of Appeal, that he is then required to set out in greater detail the particulars of the matters in regard to which the Tribunals are alleged to have erred.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The appellant only has to make fuller submissions on his appeal on the day of the hearing before the District Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I hope that this reassures Ms Rahayu Mahzam that an appellant will have ample time to seek legal advice on the appeal, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On clause 16, Mr Murali Pillai asked whether allowing a case to be reheard on a ground involving issues of fact is, in fact, consistent with the previous approach of narrowing the scope of an appeal from the Tribunals to the High Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In such cases, even though leave to appeal to the High Court has not been granted as it does not concern an issue of law or jurisdiction, it is nonetheless important that parties are provided with an appropriate and right of recourse through the reconsideration and rehearing by Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This, I will add, is also consistent with the practice in tribunals in other jurisdictions, such as those in Hong Kong and New Zealand.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On a related note, Mr Murali Pillai asked if empowering the District Court in this manner effectively gives the District Court supervisory jurisdiction over the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is not the intention nor the desired effect of this clause.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The District Court's power to remit cases for reconsideration, or order a rehearing, does not fall within the definition of "supervisory jurisdiction", and this is explained by the Court of Appeal in the case of Citiwall Safety Glass vs Mansource Interior.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If Mr Murali Pillai wants the citation, it is   1 SLR 797.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In particular, the District Court which remits a case or orders a rehearing is not reviewing the proceedings and decisions of the Tribunals below.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is merely directing that new evidence which was not previously considered, be considered by the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I now turn to the enforcement of Tribunals' decisions, on which a few Members spoke about.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While the State Courts do not currently track statistics on the success rates of enforcing Tribunals' decisions, I fully agree with Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Desmond Choo that the enforcement process must be simplified and accessible to Court users.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Tribunals have made steps in this direction.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When an order is made, the Tribunal Magistrates will brief the claimant and respondent on (a) the consequences of non-compliance; with the hope that in doing so, the respondent will be more aware of the consequences of not obeying the order in favour of the claimant; (b) the options which a claimant has to enforce his order; so right at the outset, the claimant is aware of the suite of options that he has available; (c) provide information which the claimant may consider, in deciding whether it is worthwhile to commence enforcement proceedings or not; and (d) the typical enforcement fees that he might incur.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, all these are given upfront and told to the parties at the stage where the order is made.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Tribunal Magistrates will also give parties a brochure at the end of the hearing and address any questions that parties may have about the judgment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members of the public may also approach the Tribunals' staff in person or through the Tribunals' hotline if they have any queries on the enforcement process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Desmond Choo asked if there are plans to relook the costs involved in enforcing a money order issued by the Tribunals, to make it more cost-efficient for the average claimant to enforce his order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will also study Mr Louis Ng’s suggestion to carve out separate enforcement processes for low-value claims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would add also, in relation to the proceedings, a suggestion brought up by Mr Dennis Tan that today, any individual, whether a party or a non-party to the Tribunal proceedings, can ask for and obtain a copy of the judgment, to find out what has happened and what was ruled and how it was ruled in each particular case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On vacant possession, Mr Murali Pillai raised some concerns about the enforcement of a specific type of order which the Tribunals can make, namely, the power to order delivery of vacant possession in claims for unpaid rent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This was on the basis that not even the Magistrates' Court has jurisdiction to hear and try such action where there is no claim for a sum of money.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think he is referring to section 52(1A) of the State Courts Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked if there will be safeguards when the Tribunals make this order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Insofar as Mr Murali Pillai is concerned that the Tribunals are being given the power to make an unduly onerous remedy, I would like to set out the following points in response.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Vacant possession is a usual remedy for unpaid rent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If rent is not paid, particularly when it is not paid persistently, then it is only right that the landlord has an option for getting vacant possession back from the tenant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And empowering the Tribunals to order the delivery of vacant possession where necessary broadens, in my view, fairly, the suite of orders available to ensure that justice is done.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, while it is correct that Magistrates Courts do not currently have the power to hear claims which are exclusively non-monetary in nature, they do have the power to hear claims for unpaid rent and make orders of vacant possession.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The amendments merely extend this same power to the Tribunals for claims of lower value.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I have noted Mr Murali Pillai’s point on mesne profits and double rent as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And all of that is really subject to the overarching jurisdictional limit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, no more than $20,000 for rent – mesne profits or double rent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That further enhances and strengthens and prevents any risk of such orders being made erroneously.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The various amendments and expansion of jurisdiction are likely to lead to an increase in workload.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And that, ultimately, is the overall policy objective of these amendments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked about the average number of cases handled by the Tribunals annually, and what the common types of cases were.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The common types of cases are disputes over contracts for sale of goods and provision of services, followed by claims arising from damage to property, and leases of residential premises.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While the caseload of the Tribunals is likely to increase after the expansion of jurisdiction, I wish to assure Members that the Tribunals are prepared to deal with the increased caseload, and they will also, on their own, regularly review their resources to ensure that the Tribunals remain an efficient and effective avenue for the resolution of small claims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Dennis Tan also asked what is the anticipated growth in the number of cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, there are about 9,000 cases which fall into that category.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But bear in mind that this range includes claims from $20,000 to $30,000, cases which can only be brought to the Tribunals with consent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And there are also, on top of that, subject matter limitations, in terms of the kinds of cases that can be brought.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we do not expect all of those 9,000 cases to surface in the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And certainly, that is the reason for these amendments – to drive more of the cases to the Tribunals as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Refining the Tribunals to improve their processes and enhance access to justice requires an ongoing, long-term effort.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The many helpful suggestions and thoughtful comments by each of the Members who have spoken today contribute to this worthy endeavour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, it expands the jurisdiction of the Small Claims Tribunals (the Tribunals) and, second, it improves the Tribunals’ processes and strengthens their powers to manage cases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In all, the amendments will strengthen access to justice by allowing the Tribunals to hear more claims in a quicker and more cost-effective manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Tribunals were established in 1985 to provide a quick and inexpensive forum to resolve small claims arising from disputes between consumers and suppliers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To this end, the Tribunals’ processes have been designed to be straightforward, inexpensive and quick.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Over the years, the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) has been working closely with the State Courts to review and enhance these processes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, in 2017, MinLaw supported the launch by the State Courts of an electronic case filing and management system called the Community Justice and Tribunals System (CJTS) for claims under the Small Claims Tribunals Act (the Act).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: CJTS benefits Court users by allowing them to file claims in the Tribunals with ease, monitor their case developments and even actively negotiate an amicable settlement with the other party from the comfort of their own homes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This Bill proposes amendments to expand the jurisdiction of the Tribunals and improve their processes, whilst also building on these past initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will now take the House through the key features of this Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Over the years, we have been exploring the possibility of expanding the jurisdiction further so as to allow the Tribunals to decide more claims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: After carefully reviewing this issue with key stakeholders, such as the State Courts and the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI), we have decided to expand the Tribunals’ jurisdiction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, the monetary limits of claims filed at the Tribunals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The current claim limit is $10,000 by default, which can be increased to $20,000 if all parties agree.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The new claim limits are broadly in line with similar tribunal limits in the UK, Australia and Canada.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will allow more parties to resolve their claims before the Tribunals at less cost using the streamlined procedures available at the Tribunals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, the Bill also expands the types of claims which can be brought before the Tribunals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, the Tribunals already hear a variety of claims, such as those relating to contracts for the sale of goods or the provision of services, claims in tort for damages caused to property, as well as to certain tenancy disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is in addition to certain consumer claims under CPFTA which are already being heard by the Tribunals, such as claims in relation to unfair practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The new limitation period will give parties more time to negotiate and settle their disputes amicably, whilst ensuring that there remains enough time for them to file their claims should they not settle amicably.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It is also aligned with the limitation period for consumer claims in respect of unfair practices under CPFTA, which are also heard by the Tribunals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In expanding the jurisdiction of the Tribunals, we have sought to strike a balance between the objectives of enhancing access to justice while ensuring that the Tribunals stay true to the purpose of providing effective and swift redress for small claims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If the Tribunals’ jurisdiction is expanded too far, they will have to deal with not just an increased caseload but the cases will also involve more complex and complicated legal issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is undesirable as cases involving such complex issues are best dealt with in the usual civil Courts which remain accessible and which parties can still avail themselves of.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In addition to expanding the jurisdiction of the Tribunals, the Bill also introduces changes to make it easier for Court users to determine if their claim is within the scope of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, these users have to refer to section 5(1) of the Act, as well as other pieces of legislation, such as the Building Maintenance and Strata Management Act, the Housing and Development Act and the Singapore Business Federation Act, where applicable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: So, you have to look at different pieces of legislation to then determine if your claim falls within or under those pieces of legislation and can be heard by the Tribunals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is not referred to in clause 20 of the Bill, but will continue to be provided for in CPFTA itself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To further assist users of the Tribunals, clause 2 of the Bill clarifies how the value of a claim in relation to a contract should be calculated for the purposes of determining whether it falls within the scope of the Act or not.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: At present, there may be some uncertainty as to whether it is the value of the contract or the value of the quantum of the claim that should apply for the purpose of determining the jurisdiction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill clarifies this by setting out how the value of a claim should be calculated depending on the nature of the claim being brought, for example, depending on whether the claim is for the rescission of a contract, recovery of a progress payment under the contract, or for breach of contract.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, parties typically go through three main stages when they file claims at the Tribunals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, parties will file their claims and monitor their case online through CJTS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Parties will also have the opportunity to negotiate and settle their dispute online, as I mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If it is not resolved at this stage, the Registrar will then invite parties for a consultation session where they will have a second opportunity to resolve the dispute amicably, and this I will refer to as the “Consultation Stage”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: That is Stage 2 of the process itself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill makes various enhancements to the processes outlined above, and I will touch on the key enhancements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, at the Consultation Stage, the Registrar has the power to invite parties to attend a consultation session, where the Registrar will try to effect a settlement acceptable to all parties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, if that does not resolve the dispute, the Registrar or the tribunal does not have the power to further order the parties to attend mediation even if that may assist the parties in resolving their disputes amicably.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: While this power may be exercised at any stage of the proceedings, it will be most helpful for parties to attend mediation at the Consultation Stage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: And this is in line with the Tribunals’ objective to promote and facilitate an early settlement of disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We have also proposed changes to strengthen the powers of the Tribunals to manage cases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The tribunal will identify the relevant issues in a case and will guide the parties to adduce the relevant evidence before the tribunal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will help to focus the attention of parties on key issues, and lead to cost and time savings for all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The tribunal may also direct any party to the proceedings to appear before it, summon any person to give evidence or to produce documents in the proceedings, and give directions for the just, expeditious and economical disposal of the claim.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 11 provides that while a tribunal’s proceedings are to be conducted in private, the tribunal may allow certain individuals to be present to either assist in or to observe the proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Such individuals can include mediators, whom I mentioned earlier, who can assist in resolving the claim amicably; or assessors, such as industry experts, who may have the necessary skills and experience to assess and to assist the tribunal at the Adjudication Stage to deal with the industry-specific stage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: They can also include law students from the University Court Friends scheme who are assisting the parties on a pro bono basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clauses 14 and 15 also give the Tribunals broader powers, including the discretion to: (a) dismiss a claim if the claimant is absent without reasonable cause, and I think one can see why; (b) order a tenant to deliver vacant possession of rented premises in the case of unpaid rent; and (c) order costs against parties generally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The changes I have mentioned will require the Referees of the Tribunals to play a key adjudication and case-management role in proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Last, but not least, we have also refined the appeals procedure for cases before the Tribunals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In 2005, we amended the Act to require a party who wishes to appeal against a decision of a tribunal to first obtain leave from the District Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The rationale for that change was to ensure that parties will not be put to unnecessary expense, for example, in cases where there is simply no prospect of the appeal succeeding.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This gives the District Court greater flexibility and latitude to ensure that justice is done in each individual case.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In summary, these amendments are part of our continuous efforts to improve the Tribunals’ processes and enhance access to justice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: They will enable the Tribunals to continue to fulfil their mission of providing an efficient, effective and, at the same time, inexpensive avenue for the resolution of small claims.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First established in 1985, the Tribunals provide a quick and inexpensive forum for the resolution of small claims between consumers and suppliers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill further enhances the Tribunals' bid to promote access to justice in a few ways.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The threshold in terms of quantum of claim has been raised.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a welcome update of the threshold and is not the first time the jurisdiction threshold has been amended.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There have also been important clarifications made to ensure that the monetary limit is applied meaningfully.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Under clause 13, the aggregate value of the claims of persons represented in a representative claim must not exceed the monetary limit.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While this will not restrict others from bringing their claims through the Tribunals by not aggregating their claim under that representative, it makes sure that a defendant will not face a high-stake claim that exceeds the monetary limit.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A similar restriction is applied to claims being heard together by order of the tribunal under section 26 of the current Act because of a common question of fact or law, or because the claims arose out of the same cause of action or because of the interests of justice.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another expansion of the jurisdiction is through the inclusion of some hire purchase agreements, that is, those that fall under the scope of the Consumer Protection Fair Trading Act.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Previously, cases related to cancellation of timeshare and timeshare-related contracts during the cooling-off period, deposits paid in motor vehicle sale contracts and disputes arising from a contract to buy or sell foreign currency notes made with a licensed moneychanger were brought within the jurisdiction of the Tribunals through the amendment to the CPFTA of 2008.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, at that time, hire purchase agreements were not included and, therefore, would the Minister kindly explain the previous rationale for restricting the jurisdiction regarding hire purchase agreements and why the same concerns do not arise today?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This provides a bit more leeway for parties to explore different ways to resolve their disputes before bringing the claim before the tribunal.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially important in trade relationships where parties may value a continuing working relationship more than a full and open assertion of each other’s rights.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It requires the tribunal to identify the relevant issues and to ensure that relevant evidence is adduced before it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, I would like to enquire about the rationale for imposing costs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Why is it necessary to impose costs since there is no legal representation?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What will be done to ensure that costs will not inject uncertainty into the system?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the good Senior Minister of State also ensure costs will not deter legitimate claims being brought by those who may be afraid of getting hit with a costs order?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lastly, in the series of questions, can the public be assured that any costs order will still be less than those for claims filed in the State Courts?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill also uses an alternative dispute resolution mechanism, that is, mediation, to further enhance its tools for dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 7 gives scope for a heavier reliance on mediation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Bill proposes to introduce various important amendments to expand the jurisdiction of the Tribunals, as well as to enhance the powers of the Tribunals to facilitate a more efficient and effective resolution of cases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The raising of the monetary limits will allow more claims to have access to the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is good for many people, particularly for the man in the street, who either may not afford the usual legal fees for the same claim to be tried in Courts, or may find the fees not worthwhile, given the quantum of their claim.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The raising of the monetary limits will allow people more options of bringing claims up to $20,000 or $30,000 to the Tribunals, instead of filing such claims in the Magistrates' Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Together with new hire purchase claims also under the Tribunals, the increase in the monetary limitation may hopefully reduce the caseload in the Magistrates' Courts and enhance the handling of cases in the Magistrates' Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I agree with the Ministry’s rationale to align the time bar for claims under CPFTA and also claims under other tribunals, such as the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals, as well as to allow more time for parties to explore methods to resolve their dispute before bringing the claim to the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe that the time bar of one year is too short anyway.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, I welcome the extended time bar of two years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope all these measures will serve to enhance the quality of justice at the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I also hope that, in their attempt to process cases more efficiently and effectively, the Tribunals and its staff and magistrates will always be motivated to balance the imperative of efficiency with justice and public service.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is all the more so as, unlike in the State Courts or the High Courts, lawyers are not allowed to represent members of the public using the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All claimants and respondents will handle their own claims and deal directly with both tribunal magistrates and staff.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Notwithstanding the relatively lower quantum of claims being decided at the Tribunals, I hope that the Tribunals will always ensure that both the quality of justice as well as service quality should always be maintained at a high level.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also hope that suitable training and guidance will always be given to all tribunal magistrates, including those who have not had prior or adequate civil litigation experience.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, may I also suggest that the administrators of the Tribunals consider compiling and make available to the public its decisions or judgments, not unlike the current reported decisions for State and High Courts available on LawNet.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Making such decisions and judgments available to the public will encourage better and consistent decisions and judgments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Justice must always be seen to be done in the eyes of all users of the Tribunals, whether they are claimants or respondents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope that all tribunal magistrates will exercise empathy and patience when they deal with the claimants or respondents directly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope that the Tribunals will always aim to ensure that all users of the Tribunals will go away feeling that they have been heard fairly and have a fair day in Court.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I have been calling for a review of the jurisdiction of the Tribunals since 2013 so that more people can have access to economical and expedient orders and judgment in their contractual claims.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The revision is also due as the last review of the Tribunals’ jurisdiction was conducted in 1997 and adjustments ought to be made to factor in inflation and rising costs of living.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At the inception of the Tribunals in 1984, the then Second Minister for Law and Home Affairs Prof S Jayakumar said that the objective of the Tribunals was to provide "a speedy and inexpensive machinery to handle small claims arising from disputes between consumers and suppliers".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As articulated by Mr Ong Chin Heng in his paper on "Rethinking Tribunals Justice – Serving the Community” in 2011, then a Senior Referee of the Tribunals, the raison d'etre of the Tribunals must be to serve the community and “the processes, programmes and procedures must be user-friendly and community-oriented so that end users are able to obtain the best substantive as well as procedural justice available".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I believe that the Tribunals' raison d'etre must remain the same today.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The cornerstone of the Tribunals is that the proceedings before the Tribunals are to be conducted in an informal manner.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Whilst the adoption of judge-led proceedings through this Bill would help parties to focus on key issues arising from the claim, thereby saving them time and costs, there is a need to ensure that the Tribunals' proceedings are conducted in a manner which still retains its informal nature.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Care must be taken to reduce the use of jargon and legalese and maintain the use of simplified procedures so that laypersons are not intimidated when presenting their cases at the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In 2017, the Tribunals adopted an electronic case filing and management system called CJTS, in place of the manual filing system.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To assist claimants in preparing to file their tribunal claim, there is a pre-filing assessment tool available on the State Courts' website for their use.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I tried completing the pre-filing assessment form and I was asked these questions to which a "Yes" or "No" response was required.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The questions were: are you claiming against the correct party with whom you have a contractual obligation?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Does your claim relate to a contract for services received/rendered?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Was the claim filed more than one year after the due date of performance?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Has the date for service to be rendered lapsed?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Are you seeking a Money Order or a Work Order?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I would imagine that an average layperson would find some of these questions challenging to provide a "Yes" or "No" answer to.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There is a need to simplify the language further or to provide a glossary for users’ easy reference.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: After completing the pre-filing assessment, I was given a list of notifications with instructions to read them before I proceed to file my claim.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The instructions were: please consider how you are going to support your case at the tribunal, by showing evidence or supporting documents.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: You should engage the other party to discuss remedial works or other acceptable solutions before filing your claim at the tribunal.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: You must show evidence or supporting documents to show the breach by the other party.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: You should wait till the contracted service performance date is due before filing your claim.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: You cannot bring a claim against a person or entity who is out of jurisdiction, that is, outside of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The tribunal cannot hear the matter if service has not been performed, that is, you have not brought the claim to the attention of the other party personally.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The question is: would these notifications deter the ordinary man on the street from filing his claim in the Tribunals?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While we want to expedite the claim processes, we must be careful to ensure that the Tribunals do not become too intimidating for claimants to access.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: One other area of concern which I hear from the ground is the issue of enforcement of orders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Take, for example, a case where the claimant has taken time and effort to seek recourse at the tribunal and he has successfully completed the process of pursuing his claim and obtained an order for the counterparty to pay him the sum of monies claimed but the counterparty refuses to pay up.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Those who are unfamiliar with the legal system would be surprised or dismayed to find out that they would have to take additional steps and expend more time and costs to enforce the order with no guaranteed outcomes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In a survey conducted in the UK in 2010, it was found that one in four small claims court users who won their case only received part of the payment they were awarded, while 6% end up receiving nothing.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For those which were not satisfied, how many of the orders were enforced?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Small Claims Tribunal (Amendment) Bill has two advantages.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, from the consumers’ point of view, their interests will also be better protected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, for workers and consumers, the claim process is too complicated.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, simplify the claim process to give people easy access to the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, improve the efficiency of the enforcement process.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In English): With that, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Tribunals, indeed, provide an expeditious and cost-effective way for resolution of disputes between suppliers and consumers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It may be viewed to function somewhat in a similar way to the Employment Claims Tribunal that aims to provide quick and economical solutions to smaller claims.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I welcome the notion that it frees up the Criminal Justice System and engage mediators instead of lawyers for the Tribunals.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The pool of mediators can then be enlarged to facilitate the process expeditiously.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore moves towards a digital economy, the transformation of the Courts towards digitalisation is commendable.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The CJTS provides for pre-filing assessment to determine case eligibility and, most interestingly, has an e-negotiation function where settlements can be made without going to the Court.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: But there must be assistance given to those who may not be familiar with the digital form.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The following adjustment to allow greater scope by the Tribunals is, indeed, laudable.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is necessary with the increase in cost of living and prices.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Further, it allows the Tribunals to hear more cases and, semantics-wise, this claim limit amount is still fair to be considered a "small claim".

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If the intent of the Tribunals is to provide a quick and cost-effective resolution to claims, then this amount should be periodically reviewed to be relevant to the trends and cost of purchases without having ordinary Singaporeans to incur exorbitant costs in recovering their claims in an open Court.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Section 5 – including hire purchase claims: increasingly, sellers/institutions allow instalment payments, and this is a norm that should be included in the "Nature of Dispute" as well.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Section 2 and section 35(1) – making work orders relating to property damage and short residential leases.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I welcome the step taken to enhance the Tribunals' powers and improve the Tribunals' processes.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Section 17 – empowered to order mediation which is known to be helpful in facilitating resolution.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is a great step forward and, from my experience, mediation has been effective when dealing with employment-related disputes handled by the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM) and the Ministry of Manpower's (MOM’s) Labour Relations Department.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Many disputes arise from miscommunication which can be easily addressed and settled amicably with a win-win outcome.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Last but not least, I would like the relevant authorities to create greater awareness and educate Singaporeans that there is an avenue for them to turn to if, for some reason, they are faced with purchase issues of goods and services.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Many, especially those who are less literate, may not know whom to turn to and what to do.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, their purchases may not even have relevant receipts as evidence of purchase.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: More needs to be done to empower our consumers, enlighten and educate both our consumers and our retailers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It represents an inexpensive and readily accessible way to resolve claims between consumers and suppliers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I have a few points to make on this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This would certainly give more flexibility and options to consumers, and, in fact, these limits have not been reviewed for a long time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The new amounts also make it more competitive and comparable with other jurisdictions, such as the UK, Canada and Australia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It also helps us address inflation rates and increases in the cost of living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The review is also timely to ensure enhanced efficiency and effectiveness in the operating framework.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister explain a little more on the use of mediation by the Tribunals?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Will there be plans to make this compulsory, as it is probably the direction which we should be taking?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can we also have an idea of the total average number of cases handled annually and what are the commoner types of cases that we seek?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, have there been issues with the affordability of payments amongst the low-income consumers and claimants?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There are administrative fees, legal fees, filling fees and even other ancillary fees to be considered.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There has also been a major move towards electronic filling and fixing of dates as well as appointments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The system also has an e-negotiation feature, which allows parties to negotiate and, hopefully, reach settlement on a disputed claim.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How popular or frequently is this in use?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How about those claimants who are not information technology (IT)-savvy and still need to do manual filling and have the face-to-face meet-ups as usual?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How many are those who are not so familiar with the use of the English language?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Like you and I know, interpretation can certainly lose some of the meaning that is intended.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Perhaps, some finetuning is needed in this direction to make it widely user-friendly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The new default limit of $20,000 is timely and appropriate.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Prices of goods have gone up and raising the limits would reflect the current market condition.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Nonetheless, Sir, I feel that a higher default limit of $50,000, in the absence of mutual consent, be set.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is because in many home renovations, for example, the bill often runs much higher.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, the claimant should be allowed to seek redress to at least get back some compensation, if not all of it.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Also, with more people taking up freelance and contract work in the gig economy, we can expect disputes from time to time which may well be beyond the prescribed limit.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For high-value purchases like interior design packages, high-end sound systems, the increase in claims limit is welcome relief, but it should be pegged higher as Singaporeans are proud home owners and they would spend a lot to furnish their homes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to raise this question.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Often, when we buy, say, a leather settee, the material of the leather may not be clearly described in the invoice.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How then could the claimant establish his case before the Tribunal against the respondent if he finds the settee supplied is deficient?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How detailed should the description be in the invoice?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In current practice, most invoices merely state the model number and a generic description of the furniture.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I note that disputes from hire purchase, which has been a popular mode of transaction, will be addressed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This amendment is good because, in the case of hire purchase, it usually runs beyond a year.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the case of a dispute in a tenancy agreement, most of these are for more than a year, with the option for both parties to mutually extend by another year.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Now, in a tenancy agreement, details are clearly spelt out and the document is signed by both parties, with a witness, and stamp duty paid.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this instance, apart from the landlord seeking vacant possession and any damage to the property, can he also claim for stamp duty paid if the tenant did not fulfil his full tenancy?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How is the landlord to establish the value of the property damaged?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Not many people keep invoices unless there is a warranty attached to it.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The implementation of these enhancements is insufficient when vulnerable groups, such as the elderly, lack awareness and fail to claim their rights.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They also do not have the necessary tools to utilise this avenue.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am concerned for the elderly who are less educated and who may not know what avenues are available for them to seek redress.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is more so since last year when filing for small claims will have to be done online via the State Courts' CJTS.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even the submission of documents and monitoring of case developments are to be done online.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Has any outreach programme been conducted to generate awareness among this group of people?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With more elderly living alone and having no children to depend on, how and where can they obtain assistance and guidance from the State Courts with regard to the process?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   In addition, concerned family members have shared with me about how their elderly family members would get pressured into buying things.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This particularly applies to hire purchase items whereby they are usually misled by the low upfront cost, only to regret when they realise later that the full payable amount is, in fact, much higher.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): This reminds me of the controversial goodie bag sales which sees victims, many who are senior citizens living in the heartlands, forking out $100 for various household items that they did not need.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While not illegal, the perpetrators clearly use tricky marketing tactics.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While it may not be possible to apply such a warranty to all products, it could have a deterrent effect on those who take advantage of the vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I note the Bill gives more power to the Tribunals to resolve conflicts.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mediation, as a primary resolution, is good as it relieves all parties of the time, trouble and resources from escalating the case to the State Courts.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, it becomes a cause for concern when either party uses it as an excuse to drag out the case.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will there be penalties for deliberately uncooperative parties?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is good that the amendments spell out clearly what are the specific claims that would be heard by the Tribunal, so that more claims can be heard and in a more expeditious manner.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This offers clarity for the parties to a contract.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hire purchase is a popular purchase contract for many people, and disputes may arise after the contract is signed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially if the lifespan of the product is shorter than the period of the hire purchase, or when the after-sales service is not delivered as promised.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think this is a good start, but I would like to ask that the Ministry continually review this limitation period with a view to extending it to three years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The inclusion of this clause would make the buyers aware of their rights, as well as flag out to the sellers that they have their obligations to fulfil under the hire purchase terms.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the case of tenancy contracts, which are also another high-volume contract, given that many apartments and offices are being leased out by owners, there is the limitation that the lease should be for a two-year period to qualify for hearing by the Tribunal.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For clarification, there are many contracts where the owners offer options for renewal for a third year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This limit should be continually reviewed so that it reflects the market conditions, such as inflation and the rise in the cost of items purchased.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The amendments reflect the rising costs of living and, therefore, the quantum of disputes, and also promotes greater access to justice through the quick and relatively inexpensive forum of the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Bill is introduced after public consultation on the proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The approach taken by MinLaw in involving members of public to give feedback on the Bill before it is debated here is particularly commendable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support the amendments and take the opportunity to make a few short points on the proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, sections 26 and 27 of the Act presently allows for the consolidation of claims involving a common question of fact or law, as well as representative claims or class action claims.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand that the amendments are proposed out of a recognition that the Tribunals may not be equipped to deal with a large number of consolidated claims, whose total aggregate value may exceed the Tribunals' limit by a large margin.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, there is a danger that the proposed amendments, which link the combined value of the claims to the Tribunals' monetary jurisdiction for a single case, may substantively impact on the original policy behind the statutory intent to allow consolidation of claims, as enshrined in the provisions as it stands now.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The main rationale underlying the consolidation of proceedings is to ensure an efficient hearing of related actions under a common umbrella.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This can be done through trying all the cases in one go or trying a "test case" where the Court's findings may bind the rest of the parties in the consolidated action.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Where there are claims giving rise to common questions of law or fact or that arise out of the same events, there is compelling logic to have the same tribunal to have the power to order that the claims be heard together.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Apart from savings of time and resources, there is also an issue of substantive fairness and justice, namely, to militate against inconsistent findings of fact by different tribunals arising from the same events.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am also concerned about the practical effect on the resources of the Tribunals which may consequently have no choice but to hear cases arising from the same subject matter separately.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given that the order of consolidation is a discretionary judicial remedy, I wonder if it would have been better to leave it to the Tribunals to decide whether or not to grant the order, having regard to all the circumstances of the case, including the specific kind of issues involved and whether it is equipped to deal with these issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Another intermediate solution would be to provide for a higher limit for the aggregate value of consolidated or class action claims so that a balance can be struck between the two competing policies that I have identified.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, clause 15 of the Bill repeals sections 35 to 37 of the Act and introduces a new section 35 that expands and improves the type of orders that the Tribunals may make.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the Ministry's public consultation paper, it was explained that this was to enhance the Tribunals' case management powers since sections 31 and 32 of the Act presently provides that no costs shall be awarded, save in respect of frivolous or vexatious claims.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Proceedings before the Tribunals, as pointed out by the hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza, exclude representation by a lawyer.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As explained by the then Minister for Labour and Second Minister for Law and Home Affairs Prof S Jayakumar to this House in 1984, to ensure that a litigant will not be at a disadvantage because he is unable to afford legal representation and to keep costs to a minimum, parties are to present their own case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is why it is provided that, unless a claim is frivolous or vexatious, no costs, apart from disbursements, may be awarded.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In these circumstances, since no legal representation is allowed before the Tribunals, how is a party's costs to be judged and quantified?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I believe this is the same point that was raised by the hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza earlier, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is in addition to an order for the tenant to pay outstanding rent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Notwithstanding that the Tribunals' jurisdiction is only in respect of claims relating to a contract for the short-term lease of residential property not exceeding two years, an order for possession, which may be enforced by a writ of possession, is, I would suggest, an onerous remedy against the tenant.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It also, in effect, deals with a subject matter, in form of the res, that usually exceeds the Tribunals' monetary jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, as it stands, under section 52(1A) of the State Courts Act, even the Magistrate's Court, which is a forum where parties may have legal representation, does not have the civil jurisdiction to hear and try an action where there is no claim for any sum of money or the relief sought in addition to the claim amount is in respect of the subject matter which exceeds the Magistrate Court's limit.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am concerned whether the Tribunal is the best forum to determine this issue, especially since parties do not have legal representation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Senior Minister of State would know that when it comes to orders of delivering vacant possession, it is associated with also the calculations of mesne profits in the situation of holding over or calculation of double rent under the Civil Law Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, these are issues that perhaps the Tribunal may not be able to handle.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Will there be any safeguards put in place to minimise the risk of injustice in the form of allowing such orders to be appealable as a matter of right, or to provide guidance to the Tribunal on when the power to order vacant possession should be exercised?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In addition, leave to appeal must be granted by the District Court before an appeal may be brought.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Further, the proposed amendments would allow a case to be reheard on a ground involving issues of fact.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This effectively expands the scope for an appeal, by allowing a rehearing of cases on the basis of a question of fact.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This approach seems to be different from the approach taken by the Ministry in 2005, where the then Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Law Prof S Jayakumar stated that the scope for an appeal was deliberately narrowed in order to promote finality, and to avoid the high costs in appealing that may exceed the sums in dispute.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Notwithstanding the clarificatory points I have raised, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, I welcome the move to carve out greater space for mediation for the resolution of small claims.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This recognises the value of collaborative conflict resolution that preserves relationships even where the claim amounts are relatively low.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will there be a similarly strong effort to channel most Tribunal claims to mediation first?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For claimants in civil cases, solicitors are required by the Legal Profession Professional Conduct Rules to evaluate the use of alternative dispute resolution (ADR) processes in an appropriate case.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, claimants are required to fill in an ADR form which provides them with information on ADR processes to guide their decisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that Tribunal claimants will be acting in person, often without the benefit of legal advice, will similar information be provided to Tribunal claimants?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, a Registrar now has the power to order a party to pay costs under section 35(1)(a).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify the situations under which a party may be ordered to pay costs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under Order 59 Rule 5(c) of the Rules of Court, the Court may take into account parties’ conduct in resolving the matter by mediation in ordering adverse costs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A successful defendant may be deprived of a portion of costs they would otherwise have been awarded if found to have unreasonably refused to engage in mediation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would the refusal to participate in mediation or clear bad faith participation in mediation be a ground for or be taken into consideration when ordering costs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State also clarify what sums a party might be ordered to pay as costs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given the limits on the sums that can be claimed at the Tribunal, would it be appropriate to limit the amount of costs that can be ordered against a claimant at the Tribunal?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For the average claimant, enforcement of a money order does not seem cost-efficient.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, are there plans to relook the costs involved in enforcing a Tribunal money order to make it more cost-efficient for the average Tribunal claimant?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given the efforts to align the Small Claims regime with the Employment Claims regime, would the Ministry also consider carving out separate enforcement processes for low-value claims?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In recent years, great strides have been made to strengthen access to justice to the public.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Enabling access to justice must remain a cornerstone of our legal framework, as robust and efficient dispute resolution greatly aids businesses and consumers alike.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am, therefore, pleased to hear of the amendments to the Act to strengthen access to justice in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note that in 1984, the Tribunals, through the joint efforts of MinLaw and MTI, were introduced to allow for a speedy and inexpensive machinery to handle small claims arising from disputes between consumers and suppliers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It sought to ensure that (a) there is consumer protection with speedy dispute resolution that is not belaboured by strict rules of evidence or Court procedures; (b) cost is kept to a minimum; and (c) a litigant in person is not disadvantaged by the inability to afford legal representation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As we review the existing Act, we should continue to be guided by these principles.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In this vein, I have some comments to make in relation to some of the proposed amendments in this Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The jurisdictional limit of the Tribunals was $2,000 in 1984.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This limit, over time, has been increased to $10,000.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, it is notable that the last revision on the limit was done in 1998, almost 20 years ago.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some may express concerns that the proposed limit is still too low, especially as the litigation costs, even for claims slightly above S$30,000, can sometimes be quite high.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On the other hand, lawyers may feel that more work is being taken away from them as more processes are made simpler for litigants-in-person.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note that there will always be challenges as we seek to set limits.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I trust, however, that the Ministry remains open to review this limit at the appropriate junctures.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is a good alignment with the limitation period for bringing claims in other tribunals in the State Courts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: While the inclusion of hire purchase claims is a welcomed addition, another common area of need for many Singaporeans is a platform to resolve disputes arising from personal loans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Currently when parties enter into IOUs or written personal loans, they are unable to use the Tribunals to assist with resolving their dispute.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Previously, Members of this House had also asked about platforms to arbitrate personal injury or property damage claims relating to the use of personal mobility devices.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As the needs of Singaporeans continue to change, we must constantly evaluate the types of claims that can be arbitrated under the Tribunals.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I, therefore, urge the Ministry to consider including some of these claims, perhaps in the next review or amendment of the Act.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This amendment also seeks to empower the Tribunal to award costs against parties where necessary.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Currently, the Tribunal does not have the power to make cost orders except when the claim brought forward is frivolous and vexatious.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This was envisioned to give the litigant in person with genuine claims a piece of mind to air their concerns and be given an opportunity to be heard.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Often, litigants in persons may be unable to see the other parties’ perspective easily and may be over-zealous in pursuing their claims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would urge that the exercise of these powers to order costs be done very judiciously so as not to penalise lay persons too quickly.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I also support the enhancement for the Tribunal to order mediation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As a mediator, I definitely see value in mediation being a key step in dispute resolution.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I, therefore, hope that in mandating mediation within this process, the Tribunal takes the effort to ensure that parties understand and appreciate the purpose and value of mediation so that they are attending such mediation sessions with an open mind to resolving such disputes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If it becomes clear that the gap between parties is too big, then mediation may not be the most appropriate option, and parties should be able to go through the process without any delay.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Currently, there is no avenue to appeal unless a question of law or jurisdiction arises.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This had led to some dissatisfaction by some who have come before the Tribunal.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is a fine balance between providing finality of outcome and ensuring just outcomes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It may be useful to give litigants in person more time to file a notice of appeal, especially where they are seeking determination on a question of law or jurisdiction.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Fourteen days may be too short a time to seek legal advice and prepare the notice of appeal.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As the Tribunal will be a place where the public interact with the justice system to seek recourse for their grievances, we must also evaluate the experience one goes through and, often, the experience can greatly impact one’s impression of the justice system.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I trust these Practice Directions will not take the usual form as the ones issued to legal practitioners and will be easy and simple to follow.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The awareness is a critical enabler to access justice.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In the second reading of the Small Claims Tribunals Bill in 1984, the then Second Minister for Law and Home Affairs Prof S Jayakumar said that "the primary purpose of this Bill is to provide for a speedy and inexpensive machinery to handle small claims arising from disputes between consumers and suppliers.” After 34 years, this rationale still holds true today.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Every year, CASE receives many requests for assistance from consumers whenever they have disputes with businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Wherever possible, we strive to mediate a settlement between the parties.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, in some cases, a mediated settlement is simply not possible because of the different expectations between parties.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In such cases, where the disputes concern a lower quantum, below $10,000, referring consumers to the Tribunals allows them to have their dispute adjudicated in a speedy and inexpensive manner.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These amendments will widen the jurisdiction of the Tribunals and enable more consumers to have access to the Tribunals to seek a fair decision in their disputes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The alternative is for consumers to engage their own lawyers to argue their case in Court and this would invariably result in higher legal costs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There has been feedback from consumers that when they bring their cases to the Tribunals, decisions made by the Referee were not explained clearly to the consumer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The end result is that the consumers have no idea as to the reasons why their claims were dismissed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sometimes, they feel aggrieved at the perceived injustice.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It also affects their decision whether to appeal to the High Court if they are still dissatisfied with the decision.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Could I urge the Presiding Judge of the State Courts to ensure that all Tribunal Magistrates appointed to hear disputes at the Tribunals are not only legally qualified personnel but also experienced officers who are trained to deal with members of the public who are not conversant with legal principles?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As the Tribunals will deal with large numbers of the public, this will allow the public or the businesses to better understand the reason why their case was not successful.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The next issue concerns the jurisdiction of the Tribunals which was previously defined under section 5 of the SCT Act.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Nor will it be considered provision of service as low skill or labour is involved in the supply of such rental bicycles.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The research by CASE shows that there are several companies which provide for an arbitration clause in their online standard terms and conditions.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This means that consumers who buy online would have to agree to the arbitration when transacting with these online companies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The consumers have no negotiating power to ask for the arbitration clause to be removed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, for example, if an online business makes a consumer sign up as a customer and imposes a monthly charge without the consumer’s consent, this may be an unfair practice under the CPFTA.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But if the business is unreasonable, the only way for the consumer to seek legal recourse may be to go for arbitration even if the business is clearly engaging in unfair practices.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, you cannot go to the Tribunal to seek redress.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Because of the arbitration clause, the consumer has no choice but to refer the matter for arbitration.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In a recent case, when CASE wrote on behalf of a consumer to a company regarding a defective furniture worth $1,134, the company declined to go for mediation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The company asked the consumer to seek legal redress by going to the Singapore International Arbitration Centre for the settlement of the dispute, a dispute of $1,134.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, in reply to my speech last year at the Committee of Supply debate, Senior Minister of State Dr Koh Poh Koon said that "in line with the principle of the freedom of contract, businesses are free to enter into consumer contracts, as long as it is mutually agreed to by the contracting parties".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: With greatest respect to Senior Minister of State Koh, this misses the point of why the Tribunal was set up in the first place, which is to protect consumers and to ensure that consumers have a speedy and inexpensive way to resolve disputes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The reality is that most consumers do not read the fine terms and conditions of a thick set of contractual terms when they buy something of low value.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For the Government to expect consumers to knowingly agree to arbitration for contracts of small value is unrealistic because the cost of arbitration is very high.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If the Government is intent on protecting consumers from being taken advantage of by unscrupulous businesses, surely, we can specify that businesses cannot oust the jurisdiction of the Tribunal for claims that are clearly within the jurisdiction or the prescribed limit of the Act.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I urge the Government to rethink this point and not simply assert that "consumers are free to contract".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With the rise of entrepreneurship, and also the advent of online shopping, the cases of disputes between parties are likely to rise.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The simplicity of the process and the ease of access of the Tribunals are, therefore, important.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When it comes to solving disputes and conflicts, I am a firm believer in mediation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If implemented effectively, it could stop a dispute from escalating into a Court case, saving resources and time for everyone.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Nee Soon South, we have even set up a Mediation Club and hope to train many more grassroots leaders in mediation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, while mediation is an important tool for problem solving, it may be abused as an excuse to delay resolution.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A party with more time and resources can drag out the mediation, hoping the other party runs out of resources or gives up.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on legal representation for individuals.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
