text: Lawyers are not allowed in Tribunals or community mediation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But often, the disputes are between an individual and a company.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Usually, the company will have a lawyer to advise them outside the Courts.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Third, I also hope more can be done to reach out to the elderly and vulnerable so that they are aware of how and where to get help should they encounter a need to raise a dispute.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope some form of public education can be launched to help the public to know and understand the process available to them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Disputes at the Tribunals are often those between an individual and a company.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Although lawyers are not allowed at the Tribunals and Community Medication Centres, a company would usually have a lawyer to advise them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, an ordinary person would not have these resources.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is like the big bullying the small.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can we allow ordinary citizens to seek legal representation at the Tribunals?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, many ordinary citizens, especially the elderly and the vulnerable, do not understand the process at the Tribunal.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They suffer in silence and do not dare to seek recourse.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can we strengthen public education, so that people can better understand their rights?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The changes in consumer behaviour and the nature of service provision require that our Tribunals evolve its reach and jurisdiction to remain relevant as another arm of consumer protection.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are two major changes in consumer behaviour that will make evolution of the Tribunals timely.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, services are increasingly being performed by freelancers in the gig economy for companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the media and tour guiding industry are dominated by freelancers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is especially so as the monetary value of their services increase over time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I also suggest that the Ministry can work with the tripartite partners to develop industry-specific claims mechanisms to help our freelancers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the claims process has been simplified over the years, the process can be intimidating for many freelancers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the process requires the person to identify the breach and evidenced it in writing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This can be intimidating, especially for those less acquainted with the legal process, as also brought up by hon Member Mr Patrick Tay.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And our freelancers may frequently come up against larger companies which have access to legal counsel, though lawyers cannot be present during proceedings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Establishing industry-specific claims mechanisms for freelancers may help to level the playing field.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the Tribunals can mandate certain cases to be mediated by the tripartite partners with consensus made enforceable by the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This process is important in establishing new longer-term forms of protection for Singaporeans joining the freelance industry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is also an expanding part of the Singapore workforce that operates outside of the ambit of the Employment Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Tribunals can form a key thread in the fabric of support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The other significant change to the consumer landscape is the fast growth of micro transactions involving larger groups of consumers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, there are many disputes involving customers who purchase items through Facebook or Carousell and where the expected services are not rendered properly, leading to disputes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In such instances of micro transactions involving multiple parties and claimants, it is often not economically feasible for the individual to file such claims.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, does the Tribunals allow for a larger group of consumers to file for such claims collectively?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The evolving nature of online retail is such that many consumers can be affected very quickly over a very short period of time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Perhaps the Ministry can consider for such collective action without everyone having to file individual claims, as perhaps also expounded by the hon Member Mr Murali Pillai.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Tribunal was set up in 1985 to provide a quick and inexpensive forum for the resolution of small claims between consumers and suppliers, as stated also by hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: From the perspective of the claimant, having a judgment without enforcement defeats the purpose of filing a claim.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the claimant can appeal to the Registrar to waive or defer the payment or claim the cost from the judgment, it is not guaranteed to happen.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Consumers will weigh the cost and benefit and feel that perhaps it is not worth the time and money over a claim as the original claim amount could be lower than what they would have to pay for enforcement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The process could also be complex and may take time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Hence, consumers might just give up if the amount is not large and the cost outweighs the benefits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Rogue business owners or service providers may then be able to get off scot-free.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must guard against these businesses hiding behind the veneer of cost barriers to law enforcement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Consumers must also be made aware of the difficulties of enforcing claims at the time of purchase rather than at the point of making claims.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):  	Mr Deputy Speaker, increasing the jurisdiction of the Tribunals and strengthening the claims process will help more people to solve disputes through legal channels, and expedite the process of hearing their claim.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Meanwhile, it is also a safeguard for freelancers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For many Singaporeans, especially for the elderly and people without any legal experiences, dealing with the legal processes can be very daunting.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When I tried to experience the claims process, I noticed that certain wordings and processes, indeed, require some time to digest.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, the changes to the Tribunals must occur to reflect its relevance in the new norms of consumer behaviour.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At the same time, it must strike a careful balance between inadvertently fostering a litigious society and consumer rights.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When the Small Claims Tribunal was first conceived over 20 years ago, its overriding philosophy was to provide a straightforward, quick and inexpensive way of resolving claims of low value.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That remains true to this day, and we must strive to keep to that philosophy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While I am grateful for suggestions to further enhance the jurisdiction and accessibility of the Tribunals, and we have heard many today, we must keep in mind the need to delicately balance what we seek to achieve through the Tribunals and what these suggestions might then take the process towards.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Whilst many of these suggestions are good ones, and they do take us closer to what it might be like to appear in Court, we must not forget that, at the end of the day, whilst the claims can be brought in the Tribunals, with all its limitations that we have heard about, there is nothing to stop a party from going to Court with lawyers, as Er Dr Lee Bee Wah has suggested, if they wish to, or without the limits, as some of the other Members have suggested.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we must bear in mind that at the end of the day, the Tribunals sit in a system, an ecosystem, of a series of options available to a party, and we must bear in mind at the end of the day that we are trying to reach a quick, expeditious and inexpensive resolution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And it is with this philosophy in mind that I address the concerns that have been brought up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Various Members have raised the possibility of expanding the jurisdiction of the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They suggested that the Tribunals cover other types of claims; that the claim limits could be increased; and the limitation period for claims before the Tribunals could also be lengthened.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I am heartened to hear such support for the work of the Tribunals being voiced, to the extent that my fellow Members here in this House agree, or urge, that the jurisdiction be further expanded.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, Mr Christopher de Souza's question as to why hire purchase has not been brought in is precisely one of those points, that it is now more prevalent and a lot more germane to what parties seek dispute resolution over, and so they are now part of the rubric of the Tribunals as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Ms Rahayu Mahzam have highlighted the newer types of claims arising from, I would say, new consumer behaviour – I think Mr Lim Biow Chuan mentioned o-Bikes as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These claims for unreturned deposits, yes, they do cause a degree of angst, but they are also new types of claims brought about by somewhat new advents in the new economy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And so, whilst the claims do exist, and they do need to be resolved, I think it would be necessary to study them and the ecosystem in which they occur to determine the extent to which they are suitable for resolution by the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Again, I urge all of you to bear in mind that there is nothing to stop these claimants from going to avail themselves of Court services.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members also suggested taking stronger measures in relation to cases of consumer claims that fall within the jurisdiction of the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Specifically, Mr Lim Biow Chuan queried if businesses could be prohibited from inserting arbitration clauses in their contracts with consumers which purport to oust the jurisdiction of the Tribunals to hear any dispute.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In a similar vein, Mr Saktiandi Supaat also suggested mandating that all hire purchase contracts include a clause that both parties may approach the Tribunals in the event a dispute arises within two years of entering the contract.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Joan Pereira also suggested introducing a two-week cooling-off period for all hire purchase contracts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As a general principle, the Government adopts a balanced approach to supporting a pro-enterprise environment, while at the same time protecting consumers, and I would urge Members to bear in mind that we are looking at it in a very balanced way, and not only from the viewpoint of the consumer.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is not to say that there is no recourse for unfair terms imposed on consumers today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And on that point, Mr Lim Biow Chuan commented on the use of UCTA, that notwithstanding that there is an agreement between parties, if it is shown that it falls within UCTA, the provisions can still be set aside under UCTA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Similarly, CPFTA also provides consumers with protection against unfair practices, such as pressure selling and false claims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Consumers who have reason to believe that sellers have engaged in such practices may also approach CASE with details of these practices for CASE to assist them in seeking redress.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, a key way to protect consumers and ensure they have a level bargaining field when disputing a contract is to improve their awareness of institutions, such as the Tribunals, through public education.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat queried whether a tenant who has entered a two-year lease contract with an Option to Renew may make a claim in the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That, I think, really depends on the context in which it arises, the specific negotiation of that case, and the extent to which parties have regarded that as an Option to Renew, as opposed to a fresh lease.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I am not saying that it is not covered, but one needs to look at it quite carefully to determine those legal and factual questions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On a separate note, Mr Desmond Choo asked if the Ministry could work with the tripartite partners to develop industry-specific mechanisms for freelancers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think he mentioned the gig economy on this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Steps have already been taken to enhance this area.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will no doubt convey Mr Desmond Choo’s suggestion to allow certain disputes involving freelancers to be mediated by the tripartite partners to MOM.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I turn now to accessibility and affordability of the Tribunals, which both Ms Joan Pereira and Ms Rahayu Mahzam touched on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is important to ensure accessibility to the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are three aspects to it – awareness, user-friendliness and cost-effectiveness of the Tribunals, and I will deal with all three.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, the State Courts have, through various outreach programmes, educated various segments of the public on the Tribunals and their key features.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: CASE has also been referring consumers with eligible claims to the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will look further into the suggestions raised by Ms Joan Pereira and Ms Rahayu Mahzam in this regard, as we continue to work with the State Courts to generate greater awareness about the Tribunals and improve accessibility.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, efforts have also been taken to ensure that the Tribunals are user-friendly, even for claimants who are less IT-savvy, and, as some Members have pointed out, are in need of assistance, either language-wise or expertise-wise, in navigating the judicial process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As a starting point, the State Courts provide a complimentary pre-filing online service to all potential claimants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: By answering a few general questions, claimants can better ascertain the viability of their intended claims and whether those claims can, in the first place, be filed in the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This process generates a summary of issues, known as “notifications”, which informs potential claimants of the requirements they must meet or the documents they must prepare to proceed with their claim.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This ensures, at the very early stage, that proceedings before the Tribunals progress smoothly, parties will come prepared with the necessary evidence and the documentation to support their case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Parties may then file their claims on the electronic filing system CJTS.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On that CJTS platform, parties may, one, engage in e-Negotiation and e-Settlement, as I mentioned at the outset; or two, schedule hearing dates and times in an electronic diary if the settlement is not reached; three, view their case details and correspondence with the Court; or four, submit documents; or fifth, make payment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Several Members suggested that CJTS could be supported by a hotline or call centre, and that special arrangements be made for those who are visually impaired or illiterate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One option is for them to call the Tribunals at a number that is listed on the website or available on the brochures, if they have any queries on the Tribunals’ process or services.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This hotline provides a multilingual service for users who may not speak English.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Another option is for them to go in person to the Tribunals, where there are student representatives and trained officers from the State Courts who can guide them through the filing process in their own mother tongue.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: During the hearing itself, Court staff and interpreters are also on hand to provide assistance during proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Parties who are visually impaired or illiterate may, in those cases, be represented by a third party, who may sit in with them and assist them in the course of the hearing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In relation to CJTS, Mr Patrick Tay expressed some concern that an average layperson would find some of the pre-filing questions challenging to answer.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He suggested simplifying the language or providing a glossary for Court users’ easy reference.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, as mentioned before, there are trained State Courts’ officers and also student representatives from local law schools who are on hand to assist the users.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They assist to answer questions, explain the process of the Tribunals, and manually guide them through the process of filing a claim.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That said, we have noted the feedback on how it can be further improved, and we will certainly look into it with the State Courts as part of our efforts to continuously enhance the accessibility of Court services.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay also asked if the list of notifications on the points that one should take note of before filing a claim using CJTS may intimidate or otherwise deter some claimants from filing their claims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef queried how frequently the e-Negotiation system on CTJS has been used.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Allow me to assure Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef that the Tribunals’ cost structure is specifically designed to be affordable to the wider public.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When filing a claim, a party is required to only pay a lodgement fee.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is, otherwise, 1% of the claim amount.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Further, in some cases, the successful parties may also apply to recover their fees or disbursements, or a portion of it, from the losing party.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng mentioned that in a previous Parliamentary Question, the cost was in the range of $400 to $600 for a $2,000 limit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Even in that situation, even before these amendments, the limit was already $10,000 for Tribunal jurisdictional limits.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In most cases, parties must appear in person, a point that Er Dr Lee Bee Wah raised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That, itself, reduces the need to pay legal fees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Parties, however, who require legal assistance at the hearing may also approach the Community Justice Centre at the State Courts for free onsite legal advice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, free onsite legal advice is provided at the State Courts for any user of the Tribunals who wishes to avail himself or herself of legal advice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We must also bear in mind, taking into account Er Dr Lee Bee Wah's suggestions that the model we are trying to build for the Tribunals is really one that is inexpensive, fuss-free as far as possible, and quick.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Sometimes, the introduction of lawyers into this does not quite provide for all of those.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It may be a little bit less inexpensive, and it may just take a little bit longer.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we are trying to find the right balance and the Tribunal amendments try to deal with that proposition.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members have asked about the amendments to allow costs to be ordered at the discretion of the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Today, costs can only be imposed in a very narrow situation where a claim is frivolous or vexatious.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it is really directed at the conduct of the proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One bears in mind that with the amendments that we have in place, there are three stages to the proceedings, as I mentioned at the outset.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The process can, in fact, be unreasonably stretched out by an unreasonable litigant and the discretion for costs is designed to give redress to that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Several Members have asked how we can ensure that the practice of awarding costs under the new provision will not discourage litigants with bona fide claims from bringing their claims before the Tribunals, for fear of, and I quote Mr Christopher de Souza, "getting hit with a costs order".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think these are very valid concerns.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Costs will be calculated according to the general rules, according to governing costs for litigants-in-person.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, a litigant-in-person will be reasonably compensated for the time he has expended, for example, taking leave to attend the hearing, and other such related costs, in addition to expenses reasonably incurred, for example, transport costs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, one can see that the paradigm is very different from where one seeks party-and-party costs in a situation where lawyers are involved.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In light of these guiding principles and our Courts' own experience and expertise in quantifying cost orders, as Mr Louis Ng pointed out, Order 59 of the Rules of Court already set out the parameters in which cost orders ought to be granted, we do not see the need at present to limit the amount of costs that can be ordered against either party in the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But Members should be assured that they will be judiciously considered each time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I mentioned at the outset, the guiding principle which underpins these amendments is to facilitate an efficient, effective and inexpensive avenue for the resolution of small claims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Tribunal Magistrates play a key role in ensuring that the Tribunals meet the desired goals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To achieve this, the State Courts ensure that all the Tribunal Magistrates are not only legally qualified but also experienced in hearing cases involving members of the public.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Tribunal Magistrates, referred to as referees today, also typically render brief oral grounds after each case, setting out the reasons for their decisions clearly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They also address queries and clarifications which parties may have at that juncture.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is to ensure that all parties, as far as possible, are aware of and can understand the reasons for the decision.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Dennis Tan raised the question about whether or not the State Courts will have sufficient training for these Magistrates.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Rest assured that the Courts regularly – in fact, it has been in the past and will continue to be the case – conducts training and continuing education for its judicial officers, and that would include the Tribunal Magistrates.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I note Mr Lim Biow Chuan's feedback that some users of the Tribunals, however, are not fully aware of the reasons as to why their cases did not succeed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will continue to work with the State Courts to look into how this can be improved to ensure that the work of the Tribunal Magistrates in terms of how we have come up with the decision and the views of the case can be properly and best conveyed to the users of the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mediation at the Tribunals, something that Er Dr Lee Bee Wah brought up – and I agree with her – that as far as possible, we would like the cases to be mediated, which is why it is now designed to be two-stage.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And if that does not happen, the parties can then be asked to attend mediation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That, as far as we are concerned, is the best outcome in a case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mediation facilitates the just, expeditious and economical resolution of cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Therefore, Tribunals will, where possible, encourage parties to strongly consider mediation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some Members have raised a concern about uncooperative parties using mediation as a tool, or an excuse, to drag out the case, and asked whether penalties will be imposed on deliberately uncooperative parties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The majority of parties, generally, approaching mediation, has done so in good faith, and they do so hoping to resolve their differences amicably.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some do it because they wish to see an end to the dispute, others do it because there is a continuing relationship with the party against whom a claim is being made and they wish to preserve that relationship.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, for a variety of reasons, we have seen the parties come forward, still in good faith, to undertake mediation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mediators are also trained to help facilitate constructive discussions between parties, while Court counsellors also provide counselling services to users at the same time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is difficult to legislate upfront what can or cannot be done in the mediation because mediation, by its own definition, has really got to be dynamic.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It has got to respond to the parties' needs, it has got to respond to how the parties each see their position and see their case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, I do not think it can be legislated upfront as to what should happen, But rest assured that the conduct of the parties and the way which it is going will be taken into account by these facilitators, the mediators and, ultimately, the Tribunal Magistrates.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng queried if parties will be provided with information on ADR processes to guide them on whether to go for ADR.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Such information is currently already available through pamphlets and guides at the State Courts, and it is certainly a big part of the suite of services offered at the State Courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, State Courts are not just about the litigation of dispute resolution process by going to Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: ADR is very much a part of it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, parties can also approach the State Courts staff or the Community Justice Centre at the State Courts if they have any further queries or require any guidance on ADR.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the case management powers, several Members have spoken about such powers of the Tribunals, in particular, the powers to consolidate claims, order costs on parties and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the question of consolidation, Mr Murali Pillai raised the question whether the higher limit for the aggregate value of consolidated claims can be brought in the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I can see where Mr Murali Pillai is coming from.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But this, again, is really a question of striking the right balance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Allowing claims involving a common question of fact or law to be jointly heard and decided in the Tribunals can reap the rewards of efficiency and also consistency, as Mr Murali Pillai pointed out.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the other hand, allowing too many of such claims with high aggregate values to be heard in the Tribunals may well be unfair to the respondent, may well become a very high stakes issue for the respondent, and significantly increase his potential liability, without at the same time affording him the corresponding benefit of the stricter procedural and evidentiary rules and also of the prospect of being represented by a legal counsel.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This question was also looked at by the High Court in Freely Pte Ltd vs Ong Kaili, a 2010 decision, where the Court commented that the Tribunals are not the most appropriate forum for dealing with a large number of consolidated claims involving multiple parties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The simple processes of the Tribunals were really designed for a single complainant to bring a small claim, which is relatively straightforward and not legally complicated, for it to be resolved inexpensively and expeditiously.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms K Thanaletchimi and Mr Desmond Choo also queried whether class-action suits in relation to bicycle-sharing arrangements and micro transactions can be heard in the Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will, of course, depend on the ceiling limit – the aggregate value ceiling limit of the claims in the actions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Tribunals can hear such claims so long as the aggregate value of the claims does not exceed the Tribunals' claim limit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Again, this is one of those occasions where we need to strike a balance and also, bear in mind that there is a need to, whilst allowing a claimant to bring his case, also ensure that fairness and justice are being done to the respondent who has to face this claim.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Generally, documentary evidence would usually be the best and most probative type of evidence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, it is not the only evidence which a Tribunal, including the Tribunals, can consider.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, there will be other non-documentary and non-written type of evidence available.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That also depends on the facts of the case, for example, the nature of the contract and the provisions that are in the contract itself, but I would not, by simply looking at the face of the Tribunal rules, rule it out on that score alone.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, I would like to touch on some points on appeals which various Members have spoken about.
